Hi,

Thanks for checking. This way of modelling is sensitive to precision issues. The polygonal boundary that bounds the subtraction volume overlaps with the original wall volume. This overlap is never completely accurate and hence there is some tolerance employed in this subtraction. This tolerance has been tweaked many times, hence the different results observed.

I am working on making this more robust by not relying on a generic boolean subtraction, but special-casing the polygonal halfspace subtraction and identifying the faces that overlap prior to the subtraction.

Anyway, just a message from my side to let you know your issue is being worked on.

Kind regards,
Thomas

Yeah, using `boost::` explicitly would be good. If we were to jump to C++11 at some point and not wanting to depend on Boost for certain core functionality these cases should be easy enough to simply find-in-files-replace. Picking up different implementations on compiler basis for certain classes can also cause some problems as there can be small differences between `std` and `boost` implementations (e.g., IIRC, boost has `operator <` for `weak_ptr`, but standard version is missing it). Also I think the `std::tr1` namespace will be removed completely in the next Visual Studio version, etc. The `array` use cases seem totally trivial and could be replaced with C arrays or couple explicit floats.

LongName is not an attribute of IfcProduct but one of its subtype. Therefore, e.g Spaces can have a LongName, but Walls cannot. The IfcGeom::Element describes generic products and therefore not all attributes are there.

There are two things you could do:

1 Add the things you want to IfcGeom::Element, populate here https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/master/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomFunctions.cpp#L955 and add members and modify constructors here https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/master/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomElement.h#L72

2 Use the getFile() function https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/master/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomIterator.h#L269 and IfcGeom::Element::id() https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/master/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomElement.h#L83 to obtain a reference to the instance as it is defined in the file and access whatever attribute you like.

In both approaches you will have to cast the IfcProduct or IfcBaseClass instance to subtypes in order to access the more specific attributes.

Hope that helps,

Kind regards,
Thomas

@jf-- the main improvement in terms of boolean ops for IfcOpenShell will be the new multiple operands feature. Wall openings are defined as subtraction volumes in IFC. For walls with many openings (sometimes e.g ~100), applying them one-by-one can lead to astronomical processing times. Each boolean op increases the complexity for the operands of the boolean op for the following opening subtraction.

Hopefully now this can be linear in terms of number of openings. I have not benchmarked this yet. Will keep you posted.

Hi, sorry for taking a long time to reply. As IFCOS is your baby, pretty much everything goes as long as it's consistent. :) But here follows a few of my opinions and preferences. Also in general, in my opinion, different languages don't need significantly different conventions, so it would be nice that the conventions would be similar in different languages (C++, Python, CMake).
- K&R style for braces sounds good. I also I like the modification that this style is applied for control flow but not for classes, enums and functions.
- I prefer spaces (4) over tabs, but as the whole codebase uses tabs consistently (with the exception of generated code for Python wrappings which has some inconsistency), can't think of a good reason for changing this.
- For namespaces, classes, structs, enums, and anything "constant-like" (one can't or doesnt write assignment calls for the constructs with the exception of initialization), I like `UpperCamelCase`. How about consecutive capital letters? `XMLRPCCall` vs. `XmlRpcCall`? Personally I prefer the latter as it is clearer to read, and also as the first option can lead to `ALLCAPS` which is already a typical convention for macros.
- I prefer `lowerCamelCase` for all variables, but as `lowercase_with_underscores` seems to be used pretty consistently, probably no need to change that, unless you want so. I personally don't like postfixes or prefixes for member and function parameter variables, as these are easy enough nowadays to recognize due to smart editors and IDEs, but something like _-prefix (`_member_var`), is OK for protected and private member vars. For global variables and constants (which should be used very little, if at all, preferably), some kind of prefix is OK.
- For functions `lowerCamelCase()` or MS style `UpperCamelCase()` both goes. I prefer not having get-prefix for "getters", i.e. `void Class::setValue(T)` and `T Class::value()`, instead of `T Class::getValue()`.
- Personally I dislike macros having the same convention (`UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES`) as enums and constant values as these are two totally different beasts. Macros/definitions that can leak to non-cpp files might be nice to have some kind of prefix e.g. `IFCOS_MACRO`
- In general, I think e.g. Qt has quite decent conventions IMO (although I'm not totally sure what their conventions regarding member variable naming is, probably `lowercase_with_underscores`, so "nicerFormat" for public APIs and "uglier_format" for internal implementation, maybe). Some random example: http://cep.xray.aps.anl.gov/software/qt4-x11-4.2.2-browser/de/d1d/qapplication_8cpp-source.html
- Not a fan of return types of separate lines, however template types are OK on their own line, especially when there's more than one parameter and the row length grows.
  Nowadays I like to keep the maximum row length about 120 characters, so that the commit can be easily viewed in GitHub.

> ... anything "constant-like" ...

Macros are kind of frowned upon anyway these days (although still heavily used in the code base). I prefer ALL_CAPS for constants. As this is also the convention in Python [1].

> ... lowercase_with_underscores ... don't like postfixes or prefixes.

Again, for consistency with Python conventions let's stick to lower case. I too strongly dislike post- or prefixes. The C++ standard reserves leading underscore in the global namespace. Hi Fred,

The way this works indeed is a bit under-documented. Typically in architectural drawing, floor plans are 1 meter (or 4 ft) above the elevation of the building storey. However, in IFC the building storey elevation is an optional attribute so we do not rely upon it. In fact, what happens is that a horizontal section plane is created one meter above the bottom of every product. This works well for everything that has its bottom aligned to the floor plan (like spaces, walls). Furthermore, only the intersection with this floor plan is stored in the file as an intersection is infinitely easier to compute than a projection onto this plane with hidden lines removed. This also means that products that are less than 1 meter tall do not make it to the file at all, as is what is probably happening in your case.

Needless to say there are many things to improve, but keep in mind that the SVG serializer (at least in the way it currently works) is mostly intended for simple space layouts. 

Kind regards,
Thomas

This has been introduced here: https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/commit/40a60386c8e994dfbfa594e2d5e35b870a49842e#diff-cbd871bf25fd52ab573b12d9ae80cc3cL110 in my head I knew there still was something that needed to be ported over.

The issue is that these faces are not flat, while they should be if no underlying face surface is provided. For mesh-based applications such as Solibri this does not really matter, but in IfcOpenShell a proper BRep needs to be constructed within its tolerance limits. Prior to https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/commit/40a60386c8e994dfbfa594e2d5e35b870a49842e the trick was to arbitrarily raise the tolerance, with https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/commit/884b3fe850f520a1d87ca810b440988b42824cf0 offending wires are flattened onto a plane.

Yeah this should be merged soon. Thanks for testing the caching. Caching accounts for a large part of the memory usage and in some of my tests the caching even proved to be detrimental in terms of processing time if there is little re-use, as it can take some time especially for large models to put everything in maps. Alternatively we can arbitrarily trash our cache once in a while (https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/pull/47/files#diff-4a1897ad94043892537a522bdd7fafd5R328) to prevent memory footprint and cache insertion speed to grow out of control. I will do some more tests.

Note that this is a stop-gap measure anyway as in the future I hope to do this more precisely by determining re-use by means of counting inverse relationships and depleting cache entries as soon as possible. On the other hand, this is complicated by features such as multi-threading, so we'll have to see how things unfold.

I seem to have mis-labeled my builds. I can no longer reproduce a performance gain using `std::unordered_map`. It seemed to make sense to me however: we observe longer running times as the cache grows, so introducing a map with constant time lookup should alleviate this problem. Doesn't seem to be the case and there is a weird spike in memory usage in one particular occasion. So I'm inclined to keep things a `std::map`. I didn't look into the implementation details, of which there might be more than in case of a red-black tree. Since the number of cache entries can be estimated, it might we worthwhile to set a bucket count upfront to prevent resizes and rehashes, but I don't want to invest too much time into this caching structure that can hopefully be made obsolete in subsequent releases.

Even a single iteration is beneficial as apparently within a single representation there is the most re-use, which is imaginable. I think I am going to settle on 64 as I like power of 2s. Needless to say this is very dependent on the type of file, but at least this shows it is not very sensitive to the exact value, as long as the cache is cleared once in a while. Some notes/issues about this PR:
1. Currently the Windows MSVC build uses static VC runtime which is not recommended to use if building redistributable DLLs. We should add a note/warning about this. An option for controlling whether dynamic or static VC runtime is used would be great, but that's another issue.
2. We should use a single build option BUILD_IFCOS_AS_DYNAMIC/STATIC, or similar, to control the build type of the current and possible new libraries, as is typical for many projects. IfcParse_EXPORT could be renamed to IFCOS_API or similar.
3. IFCPARSE_STATIC_DEFINE - this does not need to leak to the whole project, but can be done in the specific library build's scope, I can provide a fix.
4. IFCPARSE_NO_REGEX - not a fan of this. Modes mean harder maintainability and IFCOS uses Boost widely and if one uses IFCOS, one must use Boost too. However, these kind of utility functions could be moved to their own library. Or if the <boost/regex.hpp> inclusion leaking to client code  is a problem, we should forward declare the class in the header and move header inclusion to cpp file.
5. `__declspec` and `__attribute__` are compiler features, not platform features, so the check needs to be fixed e.g. when MinGW support is added.

(3) Unfortunately, IFCPARSE_STATIC_DEFINE **has** to leak to all the users of IfcParse. Otherwise classes would be marked as dllimport on MSVC, leading to linking errors.
If you reverse it (like IFCPARSE_SHARED_DEFINE), then everyone who uses IfcParse as shared library would have to define the macro.

(4) Regarding IFCPARSE_NO_REGEX, only a single function in IfcParse uses boost.regex. Which is in fact not called in IfcParse at all, and is even not related to it (looks like a general helper). So it is more convenient to remove it from compilation than to use boost static libraries because of it.

Regarding the exceptions: 5 years ago many IFC files were semantically and syntactically invalid in various ways and we felt that a very permissive parser, one that would just keep churning along until some exception was thrown, was most desirable. Stripping all EOLs before parsing is trivial to do, but there is one problem.
It seems that there exists a streaming mode in IfcSpfStream, it can be enabled by defining a macro BUF_SIZE. And it is not possible to add input preprocessing with this feature enabled. Well, at least it is not easy to do: it is necessary to maintain correspondence between real positions in input file and virtual positions in the resulting preprocessed buffer.
Other from that, it should be simple and relatively fast. Moreover, it can perhaps simplify parsing even further, especially the TokenString function.
BTW, IfcPlusPlus strips all EOLs and comments before parsing.

I also feel that newlines inside numbers is never generated and not supported by many programs. But a standard is a standard, unfortunately. A very long integer is indeed a highly unlikely case, but a very long float seems to be possible.

As for writing custom atoi and atod equivalents, I was also considering this option. But it is quite a lot of nontrivial code to write and debug.

Another option is to create a single std::string object, and use it as a temporary location for all the tokens (and shrink only when finished). It can be trivially achieved by making a **static** local variable in IfcParse::GeneralTokenPtr function. However, this would immediately break multithreaded parsing. This temporary buffer can be placed into some object like IfcSpfStream (or IfcFile), then it would work safely under condition that no IfcSpfStream object is used by several threads simultaneously.

Thanks for this report. The reason why some elements are not converted (there is not even an error or warning) is that they are not attempted since they are in a different representation context.

There are three in this file.

```
#4=IFCGEOMETRICREPRESENTATIONCONTEXT($,'model view',3,$,#11,$);
#5=IFCGEOMETRICREPRESENTATIONCONTEXT($,'detail view',3,$,#11,$);
#6=IFCGEOMETRICREPRESENTATIONCONTEXT($,'sketch view',3,$,#11,$);
```

While according to the standard [1]:

> The inherited attribute ContextType shall have one of the following recognized values: 'Sketch', 'Outline', 'Design', 'Detail', 'Model', 'Plan', 'NotDefined'.

[1] http://www.buildingsmart-tech.org/ifc/IFC2x3/TC1/html/ifcrepresentationresource/lexical/ifcgeometricrepresentationcontext.htm

So, `'model view'`, `'detail view'` and `'sketch view'` are in fact invalid. IfcOpenShell knows about some versions of DDS-CAD emitting this `'model view'` ContextType and therefore the representations in this context are attempted. The elements you are referring to have representations in the `'detail view'` context.

With `'detail view'` added here [2] the file converts completely.

[2] https://github.com/aothms/IfcOpenShell/blob/master/src/ifcgeom/IfcGeomIterator.h#L165

```
f1, f2 = ifcopenshell.open("existing_file.ifc"), ifcopenshell.open()
my_wall = f1.by_type("IfcWall")[0]

for x in f1.traverse(my_wall):

# For material association (layerset)
for assoc in my_wall.HasAssociations:
  f2.add(assoc)
# For neighbouring elements

My issue with boost (or in general any additional dependency) is maintenance. When building for several platforms every update has it's cost (either compiler or lib update). Binaries have to get into source control/build servers and so on to ensure reproducible builds, DLLs have to be packed with the product etc.

Binary size and slow compile times are also an issue as already stated by @aothms above - bad for iteration.

Usage of boost might vary from domain to domain, but we don't use it in our multi-platform projects (android, iOS, windows..targeting mobile and workstations). 

Here's a a list of possible, lightweight alternatives that are part of c++11 std or small enough to integrate into the codebase:
boost::thread -> std::thread available starting with c++11
boost::regex -> c++11
boost::optional -> https://github.com/akrzemi1/Optional looks like a lightweight replacement
boost::variant/optional -> https://github.com/mapbox/variant

One other option - as already mentioned in my first post is to only rely on template/header-only parts of boost and ship those stripped down headers with the codebase.
Boost BCP was made for this: http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_61_0/tools/bcp/doc/html/index.html

No that's not correct. Both scripts build the dependencies as static libraries rather than shared (e.g. `-DOCE_BUILD_SHARED_LIB=OFF` [1]). As such the dependencies are compiled into the output and are not required separately when the executable is ran. This contrary to the Docker script, that gets dynamic libraries from the package manager repositories [2].

Note that doesn't make the Docker images less portable though. The executable can be run directly through Docker on the host machine. I don't have the exact command syntax with me here, maybe @yilativs can post it here for reference.

def list_to_occ_type(occ_type, li):
    if "Array1" in str(occ_type):
        pts = occ_type(0, len(li) - 1)
        for n, i in enumerate(li):
            pts.SetValue(n, i)
    elif "Array2" in str(occ_type):
        pts = occ_type(0, len(li) - 1, 0, len(li[0]) - 1)
        for n1, i in enumerate(li):

def bspline_surface_from_ifc_advanced_face(ifc_face):
    """ reconstruct the bspline surface stored in the `ifc_face` IfcBSplineSurfaceWithKnots

    """
    from OCC.gp import gp_Pnt
    from OCC.TColgp import TColgp_Array2OfPnt
    from OCC.TColStd import TColStd_Array1OfReal, TColStd_Array1OfInteger
    from OCC.Geom import Geom_BSplineSurface

    assert ifc_face.is_a() == "IfcAdvancedFace"

    surface = ifc_face.FaceSurface

    # construct control point lists
    control_points = []
    for li in surface.ControlPointsList:
        control_points.append([gp_Pnt(*vert.Coordinates) for vert in li])

    # make sure that all sublists are of equal length
    control_list_length = map(len, control_points)
    for i in control_list_length:
        assert i == control_list_length[0], "control list must be of equal length... expected {0}, got {1}" \
            .format(i, control_list_length[0])

    poles = list_to_occ_type(TColgp_Array2OfPnt, control_points)

    u_knots = list_to_occ_type(TColStd_Array1OfReal, surface.UKnots)
    v_knots = list_to_occ_type(TColStd_Array1OfReal, surface.VKnots)

    u_mult_knots = list_to_occ_type(TColStd_Array1OfInteger, surface.UMultiplicities)
    v_mult_knots = list_to_occ_type(TColStd_Array1OfInteger, surface.VMultiplicities)

    try:
        srf = Geom_BSplineSurface(poles,
                                  u_knots,
                                  v_knots,
                                  u_mult_knots,
                                  v_mult_knots,
                                  surface.UDegree,
                                  surface.VDegree,
                                  surface.UClosed,
                                  surface.VClosed
                                  )
    except RuntimeError:
        warnings.warn("could not reconstruct surface from {0}".format(ifc_face))

    else:
        return srf

Hi,

There is nothing directly implemented for this purpose. Your options are:
* to use the parser to iterate over the polyline points and do the math yourself
* to use pythonOCC, which might be a bit overkill for this purpose, some pointers below:

Create a topological wire from the polyline:
~~~
import ifcopenshell.geom
s = ifcopenshell.geom.settings()
s.set(s.USE_PYTHON_OPENCASCADE, True)
s.set(s.INCLUDE_CURVES, True)
ifcopenshell.geom.create_shape(s, ifc_file[95])
~~~

Then the following classes and methods can help to proceed

* `OCC.BRepTools.BRepTools_WireExplorer` to explore edges of the wire in order
* `OCC.BRep.BRep_Tool.Curve` to obtain a curve for each edge
* `OCC.Geom.Handle_Geom_Line.DownCast` to cast this curve to a line (`Handle_Geom_Line`)
* `handle_geom_line_instance.GetObject().Location().Direction()` to get a direction (`gp_Dir`) for this line
* `gp_dir_instance.AngleWithRef()` to get the signed angle with the previous edge curve direction vector and reference direction (positive Z = `OCC.gp.gp_DZ()`)



Hope that helps,

Kind regards,
Thomas

As far as I know - it's not allowed to have more than one object with the same GUID in one IFC file ([_A Globally Unique Identifier [...] provides a way of uniquely identifying an object_](http://www.buildingsmart-tech.org/implementation/get-started/ifc-guid)). So, to uniquely identify any object all GUIDs must be unique.

> So, to uniquely identify any object all GUIDs must be unique.

That is also the idea the IfcOpenShell code base is structured around. For example there is a mapping in the `IfcParse::IfcFile` class from GUID (`std::string`) to a single `IfcRoot*` [1]. 

It wouldn't be overly hard though to detect duplicate guids in the parser (as the mapping is constructed anyway). Either as a simple boolean flag on the `IfcFile` class to signify the presence of duplicate guids, or a `std::set` containing the exact duplicated ids. In the geometry serializers this can then be taken into account and the node ids can be further postfixed, for example with the numerical entity instance name (`IfcGeom::Element::id()`) [2].

> Last time I worked with C++ was 15 years ago. I am not sure if I can handle it now. I thought IFCOS is written in Python. Where can I learn more about IFCOS's architecture?

IfcOpenShell is mostly C++ with a rather complete, but not 1-1 python interface generated using SWIG. Documentation on the architecture currently is sparse, if available at all.

> > Note that EXPRESS also allows for turing complete functions, which might be another story.
> Can you please provide a link so I can learn a bit more about this.

Documentation on EXPRESS is also sparse, as it is rather 'old technology' and most information is hidden in ISO documents. More intricate examples in the IFC schema are e.g. `IfcCrossProduct` which is used to assess whether an `IfcAxis2Placement3D` is valid.

> Is IFCOS using any code base from Stepcode? 

Unfortunately not. I would like the IfcOpenShell code base to be modular and to be able to plug-in for example STEPcode as a parser, but it's not likely that these more ambitious projects will take off any time soon.

> Also, BIMserver claims that their IFC is "valid" IFC which I thought they have implemented rule-checking in their database transactions.

Strictly enforcing all rules might result in a lot of files not being possible to store. In general most parsers and interpreters (commercial and open source) are quite permissive to account for some of the lower quality exporters out there.

> JSDAI project on github seems to be dead :(

I don't think JSDAI has seen any major updates after 2014 (the SDAI standard 10303-22 has not been updated since 1998), but in my experience it is well engineered. Just get it from their official site.

There are things like `IfcAbstractEntity` but I highly doubt there are thick enough layers of abstraction that you can just provide a drop-in implementation for that class using stepcode and expect things to magically work. The `IfcGeom` module would be fairly easy if there is a class hierarchy that matches the IFC schema. But differences in the way select- and type declarations are implemented is likely still going to require some significant changes to the code base. Since stepcode comes with a python code generator, maybe the Python wrapper is not the biggest concern?

I would welcome the architectural changes to make this happen. A rigorous refactoring to decouple things is planned anyway for the next 0.6 release.

A more pragmatic solution might be to cherry pick functionality your after but keep the code bases separate. What is it you would like to accomplish?

Sorry, I came a bit late to the party. I agree with your reasoning in this particular case: nothing went wrong so a non-zero exit code should not be returned.

However (and this is the annoying thing about the way the code is setup currently, and the quality of IFC files out there), you cannot really deduce that from the state the `IfcGeom::Iterator` is in. For all we know there have been exceptions throughout the processing of every representation and in that case we definitely should return a non-zero exit code.

Then the question arises, what exceptions are severe enough to trigger a non-zero exit code. As there are many forgiveable flaws in many IFC files.

All in all, I think the safest choice is the current behaviour, if no geometry is written, assume something is wrong. Plus, a successful processing is hard to capture in a single value. What we could work towards is a machine readable logging format and well-defined error codes. So that users themselves can properly judge the result.

Thanks @aothms.

I think that categorising the various levels of severity of the exceptions should not be IfcOpenShell's concern. The current IfcOpenShell's error logging system already does a good enough job in pointing at what objects (GUIDs) have been deemed problematic as far as IfcOpenShell's validation and processing goes. The rest should be up to the IfcOpenShell users and, in particular, BIM managers to chase the problem down to the original Revit (or else) file and see if that is only a problem with a slightly malformed geometry or a missing representation altogether.

On the other hand, an empty IFC file should be strictly associated with an empty geometry file and _no error thrown_, otherwise such IfcOpenShell's _exception_, will impact downstream codebases in terms of users having to deal with such inconsistency themselves.

Hi, thanks for your interest. Admittedly this all not very clear. This supported `supported_argument_types` is an unordered set of attribute types that defines the types of attributes defined in C++. In particular here [1].

All attribute types in the 2x3 4 and Alignment schemas are supported, but arbitrary aggregations of attributes are not always implemented. Suppose somebody is working on a custom schema, which introduces a new attribute with type `LIST OF LIST OF LIST OF LIST OF STRING`. The the code generator for the schema will happily emit a function that returns `std::vector<std::vector<std::vector<std::vector<std::string> > > >` for that attribute, but as there is no cast function defined in [1], it will result in a compiler error when actually using the code. This `supported_argument_types` will then filter out code generation for this attribute, so that the code will still compile, just this particular attribute will not be accessible through the statically typed schema.

The commit that caused havoc earlier that introduces the `EMPTY_AGGREGATE` type is only relevant when parsing data. In the schema, every attribute will have an element type, but the parser can encounter things like `( )`, in which case it cannot determine the type of the element. The `EMPTY_AGGREGATE` allows it then to be mapped to any aggregate (say, `AGGREGATE_OF_INT`) when the untyped parse data (namespace `IfcParse::`) is connected to the statically typed schema data (namespace `Ifc2x3::`).

Hopefully in the next 0.6 release we'll have time to work on a better approach where arbitrarily typed attributes can be paired to the parse trees.

[1] https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/blob/master/src/ifcparse/IfcUtil.h#L290

This seems to be caused by some duplicate faces in the first operand geometry. Just some of them below, there are more:

~~~
#463=IfcCartesianPoint((954.,-236.,750.))
#467=IfcCartesianPoint((2634.,-236.,750.))
#597=IfcCartesianPoint((2634.,236.,750.))
#601=IfcCartesianPoint((954.,236.,750.))

#727=IfcPolyLoop((#463,#467,#597,#601))
#739=IfcPolyLoop((#463,#597,#601))
#742=IfcPolyLoop((#597,#463,#467))
~~~

This is invalid as faces are not supposed to overlap within in a shell. In itself this is not so much a problem though for IfcOpenShell as it keeps these faces as separate constructs if `--sew-shells` is not specified.

The problem though is that later on, this geometry is used as a boolean operand (in a meaningless operation as the opening volumes do not intersect with the closed shell geometry to begin with) and for that purpose the topology needs to be reconstructed and an invalid volume is obtained. From there on all bets are off.

In this case this would be fairly easy to resolve as overlapping faces can be easily eliminated. The general problem is much harder to solve as you need to consider the possibility of multiple cartesian points with the same coordinates or the proximity of segments within the precision criterion of the model.

This will be fixed at some point, but considering the issues with the model, it might be a while until I get to it.

A more complete solution would be a non-recursive tree traversal. I'll have to talk to the OCC guys about this.

Technically, IfcOpenShell is correct here, but the reason is not overly satisfying.

The issues arise at the curved segments, which are trimmed with a parameter value of 90 degrees. However, the angular unit in this file is not properly set for degrees: `pi / 180 = 0.017453292519943295` and not `0.01745`. You're close though, Revit. The deviation `cos(90 * 0.01745) = 0.0002963267905598908` is larger than the defined precision in the file of `0.00001`. So IfcOpenShell refuses to join the segments.

So you have two options to fix this file, increase the precision on the `IfcGeometricRepresentationContext` or fix the conversion factor in the `IfcConversionBasedUnit`. Somebody should contact Autodesk about this I recon.

But there of course options to work around this as well, we can either adjust the unit if we detect it is close to `pi / 180`, but this might come at a risk. We can fill in the gap with a straight line segment, but it could introduce errors lateron due to the tiny line segments. We can also locally increase the precision.

Hi,

Wow thanks! This is a pretty good start. I think it has been a good idea to keep the changes contained within IfcConvert and not 'pollute' the conversion functions IfcGeom namespace with this. The dirtier hack would have been to introduce something like (in pseudo-code) `if (ignore_site_placement && placement->PlacesObject()->is<IfcSchema::IfcSite>()) { /* return identity */ }` here [1]. However, the PlacesObject inverse relationship has been changed into a set with unbounded length in IFC4. Therefore placements might no longer uniquely affect a site.

Some thoughts:

* One concern would be the potential precision loss of multiplying its inverse rather than simply not including the site placement in the calculation. With double floating point precision the translation probably needs to be very large, like 1e12 (?), for this effect to be noticeable.
* Another concern is that you cannot generalize this approach to other placements in the hierarchy because they are not on the 'outside' of the equation. `B^-1 A B C` is not `A C`. Not sure whether this functionality also makes sense to apply to the building placement for example.
* Lastly, as you also mention this approach only works for files containing a single IfcSite, which is probably fine, you would end up with potentially wrong results anyway when ignore distinct IfcSite placements.

None of these concerns are dealbreakers for me, but we should probably be aware of them.

An alternative approach would be to no longer convert the full ObjectPlacement in its entirety, but unroll the multiplication loop [2] when the element geometry is converted [3] when on a per element basis can be decided which placements in the hierarchy should be included. There are downsides to this approach as well. It would leave the serializer code more unaffected though. I'll leave it up to you whether you want to investigate this approach.

Hi,
Thanks for your comments. I force-pushed a new version of the branch now, where I tried something more along the lines of your alternative suggestion, stopping the `PlacementRelTo` recursion when reading the geometry. This is approach is certainly less code, and without any need to dabble inside the OBJ and DAE specific classes.

As you mention, this has the advantage of avoiding round-off errors. I like this approach better, but it's a bit scary to change logic inside `IfcGeom::Kernel::create_brep_for_representation_and_product`, especially since there are quite a few different users of the `convert` function using `ObjectPlacement`. Do you see any potential errors here? At least the logic should be the unchanged as long as `SITE_LOCAL_PLACEMENT` is disabled.

Instead of creating a `convert_placement_rel_to_site` I tried generalizing this by stopping at first occurence of a certain `IfcSchema::Type`. Does that make sense? Still, we can't "skip" an ObjectPlacement and continue at the parent, but we should be able to follow the same logic if we want to stop at another level of (e.g. `C D` instead of `A B C D`). That should enable conversion relative to `IfcBuilding` or anything else.

I did a quick test [1] on a linux vm on a meager laptop and didn't find any difference in performance with or without --mmap. I will keep it as a an option for developers and will not release binaries with this option enabled. The build scripts build the required boost libs but do not enable USE_MMAP either.

[1] `IfcConvert DC_Riverside_Bldg-LOD_300.ifc 300.dae -y --mmap? --include=entities IfcSlab`

2. Ok, so it turns out there were some minor issues I had to resolve, but those are out of the way (make sure you get the most recent commits). See the code below. Like I said, the bare concatenation of various files is rather trivial. But to get a sensible project hierarchy back is where things get complicated. I went as far as to remove the 2nd IfcProject, but depending on the use case, more work might be needed, e.g. merging up to building storey level and probably also merging the relationships (`IfcRelAggregates` in this case).

~~~py
import ifcopenshell

new_file = ifcopenshell.open()

old_files = list(map(ifcopenshell.open, [
    "Duplex_A_20110907_optimized.ifc",
    "Duplex_MEP_20110907_optimized.ifc"
]))

for old in old_files:
    for inst in old:
        new_file.add(inst)

projects = new_file.by_type("IfcProject")
# Process all but the first project
for p in projects[1:]:
    # Get instances that relate to this project
    refs = new_file.get_inverse(p)
    is_project = lambda inst: inst == p
    assign_first = lambda inst: projects[0]
    # Assign the first project wherever the other project is assigned
    for ref in refs:
        for index, attr in enumerate(ref):
            ref[index] = ifcopenshell.entity_instance.walk(
                is_project,
                assign_first,
                ref[index])
    # Remove from file
    new_file.remove(p)

new_file.write("merged.ifc")
~~~

Hi Jon, thanks for dropping by here, and again, I think we are all very lucky we have people like you at the forefront of innovation fighting the good fight. In the case of the parametric relationships I have some small concerns.

1. It seems there is a substantial overlap with **ISO 10303-108: Parameterization and constraints for explicit geometric product models**. But I don't see it referenced in IFC4. It defines similar constructs, such as:
~~~
ENTITY instance_attribute_reference
 SUBTYPE OF (variable_semantics);
    attribute_name  : attribute_identifier;
    owning_instance : representation_item;
END_ENTITY;
~~~
It's a slightly different approach (limited to `representation_item` and therefore no need for these IfcReference paths, but also basically a string reference to an entity attribute) with a whole set of where clauses to provide some checks and balances. A much more elaborate approach with also mathematical
constructs in 10303-50 to truly create systems of references of arbitrary complexity.

2. In general though this kind of introspection is very hard to do in EXPRESS and sometimes I get the impression we are betting on a dead horse. For example in ifcOWL, basically all attribute values are fully qualified instances that can be further annotated and linked, without introspection hacks.

3. In the case of `IfcReference.ListPositions` which `Optionally identifies an instance within a collection according to position starting at 1.`. Only LISTs and ARRAYs have an order, a SET is not an ordered collection and there is therefore no reliable way to index its elements using an INTEGER. That LISTs and SETs have similar representation forms in IFC-SPF is mere coincedence, other representations will not be able to numerically index into a SET.

4. General concerns about complexity, lack of modularization, ...

But yeah, I understand that there are no perfect solutions to this problem probably and I am happy to see things moving forward at this pace.

I don't think changes are necessary to the stuff in `ifcparse/`. There is a `IfcFile::Init(void* data, int len)` that you can use. See [1] how you can get a pointer and length from a `std::string`. There is handwritten code to add aditional syntactic sugar and more idiomatic interfaces [2]. OCCT 7 requires C++11, but the `"-mmacosx-version-min=10.6` we were building with does not support C++11. I tried fixing that, but it left the previously built dependencies incompatible with the new compiler arguments.

The solution now is that the platform toolset is also added to the default build path. This means everything is going to be rebuilt. If you do not want to take the time for that and you are fine with using the older OCC community edition, you can do something like the following:

~~~
shopt -s extglob
cd /path/to/IfcOpenShell/nix
mkdir ../build/Darwin/x86_64/10.6
mv ../build/Darwin/x86_64/!(10.*) ../build/Darwin/x86_64/10.6
USE_OCCT=False python build-all.py
~~~

That *something* might matter. Some features have been gradually added over time to the 0.5 version. I advise you to get the latest version.

> No existence of tesselate() or serialize() ... `make_shape_function()`

`make_shape_function` is introduced at the same time as `serialise` and `tesselate`. If you have one you have the others was well.

>  Do I have to call the whole script (main.py) or just the method, make_shape_function ?

`make_shape_function()` is a helper function (a higher order function, like a python decorator). It is not intended to be called by end users.

`serialise()` and `tesselate()` return a `IfcProductDefinitionShape` that you can assign to a product representation. For example.

~~~
ifcfile = ...
my_shape = ...
my_wall = ifcfile.createIfcWall(GlobalId='...', ...)
my_wall.Representation = ifcopenshell.geom.tesselate(my_shape)
~~~

Ah I see now, there's actually two flaws:

* we never check whether `zmin < (storey_elevation.get() + 1.) < zmax`
* `(zmax - zmin) < 1.` does not need to be true in case `section_height` or `storey_elevation` is true.

Here's what I would propose:

1 `if (zmin == inf) continue` (just to early on filter out empty geometry)
2 set `cut_z` according to current 3-branch logic [0]
3 `if (zmin > cut_z || zmax < cut_z) continue`;

[0] with one addition, `if (storey_elevation)` should probably read `if (storey_elevation && !(zmin > *storey_elevation || zmax < *storey_elevation))` in order to fall back to `zmin + 1.` in case the elevation of the storey somehow does not align with the element geometry.

0. `cd win`

There is no setting for this in IfcOpenShell, Z is always up (contributions are welcome to specify this behaviour from the command line)

When not using pythonocc, discard normals and join vertices that belong to different faces

When not using pythonocc, multiply ObjectLocation matrix into geometry vertex positions

Implied when using pythonocc, do not triangulate.

This isn't actually an entity, but rather an attempt by the exporter to print out floating points that are NaN (`-1.#IND` or `1.#IND`). And yes, it's not legal STEP-21.

We've seen them from time to time from old Revit exporters, but they happen so rarely that it's usually easier to ask people to export with other parameters or a newer version of the exporter.

Typically there's no sensible way to recover the object that contains NaN's, except erroring out/warning and move on. There are some theoretical exceptions, e.g. if a single point is broken, you can remove the faces that contain the point and hope the result is somewhat useful. I haven't tried that, but it sounds scary to emit only "good" parts of objects.
I'd suspect this is the same problem as encountered here: https://github.com/IfcOpenShell/IfcOpenShell/pull/375 Can you update to newer PoweShell and try again?

> ARCHICAD-64 21

ArchiCAD 21 is just one release behind the most recent one I think. Might be worthwhile to file a bug report somewhere with them. Contrary to e.g. Revit they don't use Jotne EDM or so perhaps they have their own floating point formatting routine and apparently delegate this to MSVC's implementation of `sprintf()`.

> but it sounds scary to emit only "good" parts of objects.

That's not so different from what happens in IfcOpenShell and the other implementations. At least IfcOpenShell does so with sufficient log messages. I think a strict mode would be nice to have, but would leave output for most files empty I think.

The `#` probably trips up the lexer (IfcOpenShell does not really have one, but rather some heuristics to read through the file efficiently). A better error message can probably be generated as `#` should always follow some digits (`ENTITY_INSTANCE_NAME := "#" <DIGIT> (<DIGIT>)*`), but not sure if this is worth the effort.

```python

from ifctester import ids
f = api.run("project.create_file", version="IFC4X3_ADD2")
api.run("root.create_entity", f, ifc_class="IfcProject")
api.run("root.create_entity", f, ifc_class="IfcWall", predefined_type="SOLIDWALL")
for opts in (["SOLIDWALL", "USERDEFINED"], ["SOLIDWALL", "PARTITIONING"]):

    s.applicability.append(ids.Entity(name="IFCWALL"))
    s.requirements.append(ids.Entity(name="IFCWALL",

    i = ids.Ids(title="probe"); i.specifications.append(s); i.validate(f)
    print(opts, s.status)

We hit it in a project-wide IDS for a small house model (a textbook example): terrain, a tree and seven `IfcEarthworksCut` failed on "The predefined type ... does not meet the required type" although their types were listed. Removing `USERDEFINED` from the enumerations was our workaround; the change in this PR would make it unnecessary.

We hit this independently on real-world production IFC models (building models with 1000+ elements each, repeatedly opened via a server-side API) and it was serious enough in practice that we built and tested a fix. Sharing in case it's useful, since @petruconduraru's root-cause analysis above (empty `ifcopenshell::file::~file()`, `in_memory_file_storage` with no destructor since 4c13e2424c) matches exactly what we found.

**Independent confirmation (Frida + heaptrack, Linux x86_64, 0.9.0.post1):** on a 17.3 MB / 1123-element IFC model, each `ifcopenshell.open()` + drop (even with explicit `del` + `gc.collect()`) permanently retains ~52 MB, scaling linearly at ~93 unbalanced allocations / ~3.4 KB per IFC element. One-shot allocation attribution for a smaller synthetic file (200 walls, 18684 blocks / 690 KB leaked) breaks down as:
- 25.6% `ifcopenshell::impl::in_memory_file_storage::index_lazily(...)` (40 B blocks)
- 10.3% `variant_array<...>::set<const std::string&>` (32 B)
- 9.8% `variant_array<...>::set<const std::vector<...>&>` (24 B)
- 3.5% `in_memory_file_storage::resolve_instance_references(...)`
- remainder unmapped to a module symbol (stripped build, same size-class profile)

All small blocks (24-40 B), consistent with per-instance attribute storage (strings/aggregates/indices) created in `in_memory_file_storage` and never released when the owning `file` is dropped.

**Fix we built and tested:** rather than patching `~file()`/`~spf_header()` to eagerly delete instance data (our first attempt - caused 13 use-after-free SIGSEGVs across common patterns like `el.file.by_type(...)` or geometry iteration after `del f`, since raw-pointer Python proxies to `express::base` can outlive the owning file), we added a small lifetime-tracking layer at the SWIG boundary (`ifcwrap/utils/lifetime.i`, redefining `SWIG_NewPointerObj`) that keeps a `file* -> {owners, handles}` registry: the C++ storage is only actually released once every live Python proxy referencing it is gone, not just when the `file` object itself is dropped.

Results vs. original 0.9.0.post1, on a 62 MB / ~780k-instance real building model:
- RSS after 3 open/drop cycles: ~49 MB (with `malloc_trim`) vs. ~2181 MB original - leak eliminated.
- 27/28 of our use-after-free stress scenarios behave correctly (vs. 0/28 "safe" on original - it silently returns wrong/empty results instead of crashing; 1 scenario, ifcclash on a dropped file, doesn't work in either version).
- Our own application's ~2200-test subset: RSS stayed flat (~2.8 GB peak vs. ~4-9+ GB and climbing on unpatched), confirming the leak fix holds at scale. However, on that same broader run we also saw a handful of test failures (6 in one module dealing with slab/wall support assignment, 2 in a geometry-check module) that were NOT present on the unpatched library - we had earlier validated geometry as byte-identical on a narrower, targeted regression set, so this is a real discrepancy we haven't root-caused yet (possibly a version-base mismatch between when the patch was built and the current code, or an actual edge case the lifetime-tracking approach handles differently). **Flagging this explicitly so nobody treats the patch as production-ready without re-verifying on their own test suite** - we're investigating further on our end.
- Cost: ~+25% on `by_type` call overhead (proxy creation bookkeeping), no measurable cost on attribute access/traverse/get_info; file release itself is slower (1.9s vs 0.56s original) since it now walks live handles instead of doing nothing.
- Known remaining gap: instances removed via `file.remove()` are not reachable from any index and still leak (~0.8 MB per 5700 removes in our stress test) - same in original and in our patch.

This is currently a local patch (not rebased against current main, and the earlier `IFOPSH_SAFE_INSTANCE` approach from #9624 was rejected for a ~12-24% parsing / ~86% traverse regression, which ours doesn't have since it only adds bookkeeping at proxy creation, not on every access). Patch + a more detailed writeup of three iterations (v1 naive free, v2 current approach, v3 refinement) here, as a starting point rather than a ready-to-merge PR given the open question above: https://gist.github.com/nierob-cmd/96aabb7573da8dee14c422f2612a168e

Happy to dig into the test discrepancy and report back, and to clean this up into an actual PR against current main if that ends up panning out.

Follow-up on the earlier caveat about a handful of test failures on our broader regression suite: root-caused and fixed, and it was on our end, not the patch.

Our local build of the lifetime-tracking patch had been compiled with `WITH_CGAL=OFF` / `WITH_MANIFOLD=OFF` (we hadn't needed either geometry kernel for our original leak-reproduction/stress tests). In the days since, our own application added a feature that calls into the CGAL-backed code path for certain composite/layered geometry cases. Testing the patch against that newer application code surfaced failures that looked like a correctness regression in the patch, but were really just that missing kernel - our patched build was simply incomplete for what our current code needed, independent of the memory-leak fix itself.

Rebuilt with `WITH_CGAL=ON` (Manifold wasn't needed - CGAL alone was sufficient) and reran: all previously-failing tests now pass (11/11, including the full module that had regressed). RSS stayed flat on a large subset we got through before a local resource constraint (unrelated, our host's own memory guard) cut the run short - no sign of the leak returning and no new failures in what completed.

So: the lifetime-tracking approach (v2/v3) holds up; the earlier scare was a build configuration gap on our side, not a flaw in the patch. Still happy to help turn this into a proper PR against current main if that's useful.
